papers.title: Manifold-Constrained PET Reconstruction with Learned Flow-Matching Priors
papers.abstract: Image reconstruction for positron emission tomography (PET) is an ill-posed Poisson inverse problem. In this work, we introduce an unsupervised, optimization-based reconstruction framework that employs a flow-matching generative model as a learned manifold prior. We train the generative model on high-quality PET images to learn a differentiable ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based transport from a Gaussian latent distribution to the PET image distribution. We incorporate this generator as an explicit manifold constraint into a regularized Poisson likelihood formulation. To solve the resulting problem, we develop an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) algorithm that integrates an expectation-maximization (EM)-type surrogate update for Poisson data fidelity with gradient-based latent-space optimization. Numerical simulations and in vivo PET experiments demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy compared with conventional reconstruction methods and recent deep learning-based approaches, particularly in low-count settings, with competitive computational efficiency.

papers.title: Toward Interaction Dynamics: A Predictive Framework for Safe Physical Human Robot Interaction
papers.abstract: Physical human-robot interaction requires yielding transiently to contact yet recovering the commanded reference under sustained load. Finite-stiffness impedance control retains a static deflection there, while predictive alternatives typically optimize a nonlinear model online. Operational-space cancellation instead exposes a translational error double integrator with a fixed transition matrix and a configuration-scheduled input map, making interaction a predictive quantity. We build on it a compact offset-free interaction-error MPC for torque-controlled manipulators: a force-domain random-walk state estimates persistent interaction and model error, and a 30-variable convex QP maps the correction through the current task inertia while constraining the applied joint torque. Conditional results establish impedance equivalence of the unconstrained passive feedback, offset-free regulation at feasible frozen configurations, and quadratic stabilizability of the scheduled backbone. In a 1 kHz MuJoCo simulation of a 7-DOF Franka FR3, the estimator cuts steady-state error under a repeated 15 N step from 2.73 mm to 0.033 mm when added to the otherwise identical 100 Hz MPC, at unchanged peak joint power. A stiffness-and-damping-calibrated impedance baseline attains 2.63 mm at the same actuator cost, and 1.36 mm with ideal measured-force cancellation, so constant-load rejection is not unique to MPC; the sensorless controller still reaches 0.033 mm. The torque constraint holds the command inside a budget tightened to the lowest the task can meet, at no tracking cost. On a physical UR5e, five alternated pairs under a nominal 1.5 kg hanging load give 1.505 mm without the estimator; with it the controller is offset-free, its 0.023 mm error being the noise level of the encoder-based position measurement. A tuned anti-windup integral also removes the offset, with larger transients.

papers.title: Dynamic infrared thermography and computed tomography angiography fusion for DIEP flap perforator selection: a novel measurement system
papers.abstract: Accurate perforator selection is critical for successful deep inferior epigastric artery perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction. While computed tomography angiography (CTA) provides high-resolution anatomical detail, it lacks functional perfusion assessment. Dynamic infrared thermography (DIRT), in contrast, captures superficial rewarming dynamics but lacks objective anatomical validation. This study presents a standardized multimodal measurement system enabling automated fusion of DIRT with CTA-derived perforator coordinates. The framework integrates controlled thermographic acquisition, real-time hotspot detection, metric spatial calibration, and global one-to-one assignment of thermal hotspots to CTA perforators within a predefined periumbilical region of interest. The workflow was evaluated in 12 patients. Of 46 CTA perforators within the region of interest, 84.8% were successfully linked to thermographic hotspots, with a median spatial offset of 14.74 mm. Automated assignment excluded 76.1% of detected hotspots due to lack of anatomical correspondence, thereby reducing subjective interpretation. The proposed system enables quantitative multimodal validation of functional and anatomical imaging and provides objective support for perforator selection in clinical practice.

papers.title: A Soft Sponge-Pillar Electrode Platform for Motion-Tolerant Ambulatory EEG and Sleep Monitoring
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiological recording systems are essential for both clinical and real-world environments. While a wide range of wearable devices have been reported for electrocardiogram (ECG) and electromyogram (EMG) recording applications, most electroencephalography (EEG) measurements still require subjects to remain stationary while wearing rigid and uncomfortable equipment. Here, a soft and wearable sponge pillar EEG electrode is presented for long-term and motion-tolerant EEG recording. The electrode is composed of two layers of a carbon black (CB)-polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) composite, where a firmer solid base assists in bypassing hair, enabling stable access to the scalp, while a porous sponge tip ensures comfort, reliable contact, and low skin-electrode impedance. Fabricated via a sugar templating process without microfabrication steps, the microporous sponge structure offers low modulus and significantly enhances the contact area with the skin when loaded with conductive gel. This allows the electrode to achieve a lower contact impedance of $1.62 \times 10^{4}\,\Omega$ at 10 Hz, outperforming conventional gelled electrodes while maintaining gel stability for over 18 hours. With the electrodes integrated into wearable form factors such as headbands, headphones, and baseball caps, EEG signal recording during motion have been demonstrated, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 16.46 dB. These features establish the sponge pillar electrode as a promising platform for next generation wearable EEG systems, enabling comfortable, stable, and prolonged brain signal acquisition on ambulatory subjects and in naturalistic environments.

papers.title: Fluid exchange and renewal in the left atrial appendage
papers.abstract: Fluid exchange through the opening of a cavity does not uniquely determine how the cavity is washed out. We investigate this phenomenon in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a deforming side cavity of the heart, using simulations of 17 patient-specific atria with wall motion reconstructed from time-resolved computed tomography. Fluid exchange through the LAA ostium is decomposed into a component driven by LAA volume change and a component due to simultaneous bidirectional flow, with no net volume transport. Washout of a scalar initially confined to the LAA is compared with predictions from two well-mixed washout models and assessed alongside residence-time distributions. Volume-driven transport accounts for approximately 24-78% of total exchange across the simulated atria. Relative washout efficiencies are approximately 26-53% with respect to the inflow-driven washout model that assumes scalar-free inflow. A scalar-balance decomposition identifies two contributions to this discrepancy: re-ingestion of previously expelled scalar and preferential export of scalar-poor fluid. Both effects reduce the effective washout rate in every configuration. Residence-time distributions reveal coexisting distinct younger and older fluid regions, and a regional analysis of one appendage localizes the older population predominantly in its distal region. These findings show that substantial exchange across the LAA ostium coexists with prolonged distal retention. Effective renewal depends on how much fluid crosses the ostium and which fluid is exchanged.

papers.title: Multi-echo AxCaliberSMT: Mapping effective axon radius from restricted diffusion and radius-dependent intra-axonal T2
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based axon radius r mapping preferentially detects larger axons since restricted-diffusion contrast scales with r^4, limiting sensitivity to thin axons dominating human white matter (WM). Surface relaxation provides complementary sensitivity through an intra-axonal R2 proportional to 1/r. We combined these mechanisms to broaden the dynamic range of radius estimations. Multi-echo AxCaliberSMT (ME-AxCaliberSMT) models spherical-mean diffusion-relaxation signals using cylinder-restricted diffusion and histologically calibrated surface relaxation. Simulations compared its accuracy and robustness with AxCaliberSMT and a diffusion-filtered R2 model, which infer radius solely from restricted diffusion and intra-axonal R2, respectively. Five healthy adults were scanned on Connectome 2.0 (C2; 500 mT/m), and four also on Cima.X (200 mT/m), using multiple b-values at two diffusion times, each paired with a different echo time. Diffusion and relaxation contrasts were comparable at a protocol-dependent transition radius (C2: 1.42 um; Cima.X: 1.85 um). Below this threshold, relaxation dominated, yielding effective r estimates approximately <r^2>/<r> in most WM. At SNR 40, ME-AxCaliberSMT achieved normalised bias $\pm$6%, whereas AxCaliberSMT overestimated small radii. ME-AxCaliberSMT was less sensitive to tested calibration errors than the R2 model. In vivo, ME-AxCaliberSMT bundle radii on C2 were 0.30-0.51 um (AxCaliberSMT: 1.03-1.38 um) and followed the histological pattern along the corpus callosum. ME-AxCaliberSMT estimates correlated between scanners (mean Pearson correlation 0.73), unlike AxCaliberSMT (-0.23), although Cima.X values were systematically higher. Combining diffusion and relaxation extends axon radius mapping from large to small axons. Translation to a commercial high-gradient scanner reproduced bundle-wise patterns, although absolute estimates remained protocol-dependent.

papers.title: SPLAT: An Event-Specific System Response Model for Continuous-Domain List-Mode TOF PET
papers.abstract: Modern position-sensitive PET detectors provide continuous estimates of photon interaction position and event-specific timing, energy, and depth-of-interaction (DOI) information. We introduce Spatial Probability Localization and Transformation (SPLAT), a continuous-domain, event-specific projection model for time-of-flight (TOF) list-mode PET. Each coincidence is represented by a three-dimensional spatial response kernel incorporated into consistent forward and adjoint operators without detector-coordinate binning. While supporting general response distributions, we develop an anisotropic Gaussian implementation whose center is determined by measured interaction positions and TOF difference, and whose full covariance follows from propagating measurement uncertainties through event geometry. The model accounts for DOI, photon non-collinearity, and energy-dependent, correlated, and depth-dependent detector responses. Using GATE Monte Carlo simulations with known annihilation positions, we compare continuous and virtually segmented representations of identical accepted coincidences. Event-localization diagnostics and point-source and brain-phantom reconstructions assess model accuracy and image formation. The Gaussian formulation also yields information-equivalent count gain, an approximate measure of relative spatial information accounting for localization uncertainty and detection efficiency. Results support the value of event-specific modeling, particularly measured DOI, while an optimized GPU implementation demonstrates computational feasibility. SPLAT provides a flexible framework for incorporating detailed detector measurements directly into PET reconstruction.

papers.title: Multimodal assessment of the skin biomechanical properties during wound healing and hyaluronic acid response
papers.abstract: Various methods such as elastography or mechanical testing have been developed to quantify the mechanical properties of soft tissues, which are related to the tissue local pathophysiological conditions. This study is the first one to investigate the in vivo performances of the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to characterize the biomechanical behavior of skin during physiological mechanisms. A murine model (12 Sprague-Dawley rats) was considered and various measurements of skin mechanical properties were conducted on different regions of interest over a 3-week period. The effects of wound healing after full-thickness excisional wound and an intradermal hyaluronic acid (HA) injection were monitored using IBAM, as well as two commercially available devices: Cutometer__ and MyotonPro__. The indicators $\Delta$t (from IBAM), R0 and R5 (from Cutometer__) vary significantly as a function of wound healing time, which corresponds to a stiffening of healing tissue compared to healthy tissue. The indicator $\Delta$t and S (from MyotonPro__) are significantly different when HA was injected compared to healthy tissue, which also corresponds to less stiff tissue. Additionally, both IBAM and Cutometer__ detect significant biomechanical variations in superficial soft tissue related to tissue growth in all measurement regions. This first in vivo use of IBAM shows that IBAM could assess significant variations related to wound healing or regeneration mechanisms following HA injection. This study paves the way for the development of a simple, low-cost and objective device. Future clinical studies or other animal models should be carried out to confirm these results.

papers.title: Detecting the pterygomaxillary disjunction using an instrumented hammer: A cadaveric study
papers.abstract: Background: In many maxillofacial surgeries, the surgeon must perform a pterygomaxillary disjunction in order to separate the jaw from the skull. The disjunction is performed using an osteotome which is impacted with a hammer until its tip crosses through the pterygoid plates. To determine whether the disjunction has occurred and avoid complications, surgeons still rely on their proprioception. Methods: The aim of this study is to validate a vibroacoustic set-up constituted by an instrumented hammer equipped with a force sensor, aiming at detecting if the disjunction has occurred. To do so, fourteen osteotomies were performed in anatomical subject jaws. For each impact, the force signal was recorded and analyzed. A classification algorithm (Support Vector Machine method coupled with a cost matrix) was developed based on indicators extracted from the signal to determine whether the disjunction had occurred. Impacts were classified into two classes, one before and the other after the osteotome had crossed the pterygoid plates. To avoid undetected disjunctions a cost matrix was added to the algorithm. The coefficients from the matrix were chosen using by minimizing the Negative Likelihood Ratio. Findings: The algorithm was able to distinguish impacts before and after the disjunction with an accuracy of 96 %. Moreover, the instrumented hammer was able to detect the disjunction with a maximum delay of two impacts. Interpretation: These results pave the way for the development of a per-operative decision support system for the pterygomaxillary disjunction.

papers.title: Using an instrumented hammer to predict the lateral hinge fracture in high tibial osteotomy: A cadaveric study
papers.abstract: Open-wedge High-Tibial Osteotomy is the most commonly employed technique addressing varus knee osteoarthritis. During this procedure, the osteotome passes through cortical and trabecular bone. A common complication is lateral hinge fractures, which depends upon when the surgeon stops impacting the osteotome. The aim of the present study is to determine whether an instrumented hammer can be employed to detect (i) the bone type (cortical or trabecular) surrounding the osteotome tip and (ii) when bone is fractured by the osteotome. Seventeen lower-limb specimens were obtained from nine fresh human anatomical subjects. The osteotome was impacted using the instrumented hammer until rupture. Each impact signal was recorded and analyzed. An algorithm was developed to detect the transitions between cortical and trabecular bone and vice versa. Detection was based on the relative variation of $\tau$ derived from the force signal as a function of time as the time difference between the second___and___first impact peaks. The values of $\tau$ were significantly lower in cortical bone compared to trabecular bone. Considering the arrival of the osteotome tip in trabecular bone during a medial, a difference of less than 2 impacts between the surgeon and the algorithm was obtained for 71% of the cases. For the lateral osteotomy it was obtained in 81% of the cases. This cadaveric study demonstrated that the instrumented hammer could prevent impacts leading to hinge rupture, which suggests that future clinical trials are warranted.

papers.title: The relationship between junctional zone, smooth muscle tone and intra-uterine pressure
papers.abstract: The junctional zone is a thin low contrast region of the inner myometrium, visible on T2weighted MRI images. Investigators have long sought histologic particularities of this region. Here, we summarize evidence that this region's specific appearance is not due to a particular tissue composition, but is a reflection of underlying smooth muscle activity. Smooth muscle tone in the spirally fibered myometrium wrings out blood and interstitial fluids to create a static low-contrast T2 region around the myometrium, while phasic smooth muscle contractions create transient, propagative low-contrast waves. We show that the competition between centripetal inhibitory adrenergic innervation from the serosa and centrifugal excitatory hormonal gradients from the endometrium divides the uterus in a tonic inner-and a quiescent outer-region. Bridging MRI and manometry studies, we discuss the relation between smooth muscle activity and intra-uterine pressure. Dysregulation of nerve and/or hormonal activity can result in a thicker tonic smooth muscle layer, entailing a thicker junctional zone and high intrauterine pressures characteristic of dyscontractility in severe dysmenorrhea, endometriosis and adenomyosis.

papers.title: Complementary-Aperture Pulse Sequencing for Fundamental-Band Nonlinearity Parameter Imaging
papers.abstract: The depletion method (DM) enables the estimation of the acoustic nonlinearity parameter, B/A, in pulse-echo ultrasound using fundamental-band signals from low- and high-pressure acquisitions, but requires accurate knowledge of the acoustic-pressure scaling factor. This requirement limits experimental translation because of the slightly nonlinear scaling between excitation voltage set on the ultrasound system and pressure at the probe. We propose a complementary-aperture pulse sequence (CAPS) that recovers the linearly scaled low-pressure signal by coherently summing radio-frequency acquisitions from interleaved transmit subapertures, whereas a full-aperture transmission provides the high-pressure signal maintaining the same excitation voltage configured in the ultrasound system. In silico phantoms of a homogeneous sample and a reference evaluated four aperture partitions of CAPS and compared them with the DM under relative scaling factor errors from 0.01% to 10%. Using the DM, errors of 0.1% and 1% produced absolute B/A biases of up to 27.3% and 58.3%, respectively. CAPS yielded mean B/A values of 8.9 for a prescribed value of 9, with biases of less than 1.3% across all partitions, matching an ideally calibrated DM. These results demonstrate that CAPS preserves depletion-based B/A estimation without using the pressure scaling factor as a reconstruction input, supporting experimental and in vivo implementation without pressure-ratio calibration.

papers.title: APHABAMAS: An analytical phantom-based scheme for assessing the accuracy of high-resolution 3D MRI motion-artifact simulations
papers.abstract: Purpose: Motion compromises the utility of high-resolution 3D MRI. Deep learning-based methods have shown promise for mitigating motion-induced artifacts, but their development typically requires simulated motion-corrupted data. Several open-source tools exist for this task. They share a common formulation but implement this formulation with different algorithms. It is unclear which algorithm implements the formulation more accurately. This study aims to develop a scheme to answer this question. Methods: The essential ingredient of the desired scheme is a ground-truth reference that does not suffer from sampling-induced error. To meet this requirement, the proposed scheme, APHABAMAS, leverages a digital phantom whose image- and Fourier-domain representations can be expressed analytically under arbitrary rigid-body transformations. APHABAMAS is used to quantify sampling-induced errors of three existing algorithms under synthetic and tracking-data-derived motion trajectories at different motion severity levels. Results: All three algorithms produce distinct but visually plausible artifacts, demonstrating the need for a ground-truth reference. APHABAMAS shows that the algorithm utilizing the uniform-to-non-uniform (Type-2) Non-Uniform Fast Fourier Transform (NUFFT) provides the most consistent agreement with the ground-truth reference across motion types and severity levels. For the non-uniform-to-uniform (Type-1) NUFFT-based algorithm, agreement with the ground-truth reference deteriorates substantially with increasing motion severity. Conclusion: APHABAMAS provides a rigorous tool for assessing how accurately algorithms implement the common formulation for simulating motion artifacts in high-resolution 3D MRI. It enables accuracy-based ranking of the three assessed algorithms, thereby facilitating informed selection of the most suitable one for synthesizing motion-corrupted data.
